newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street Journal to appeal court order.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street Journal to appeal court order.

text.p: The publishers of The Wall Street Journal said on Friday they would appeal a preliminary injunction barring the newspaper from calling a regional weekly section "California Journal."
"The ruling will be appealed. The company will seek a stay of the order," said Lawrence Budgar, spokesman for Dow Jones & Co Inc, which publishes the business daily.

The Wall Street Journal this month launched a weekly section of state business news in its California editions, calling it "California Journal." But a Sacramento-based monthly magazine of state politics by the same name, founded in 1970, sued Dow Jones to stop it from using the name.
A California judge issued a preliminary injunction on Thursday barring The Wall Street Journal from calling its weekly section "California Journal."

Unless overturned, the preliminary injunction would prevent The Wall Street Journal from using the title until a trial is held to decide the issue permanently. Sacramento Superior Court Judge Earl Warren Jr. said The Wall Street Journal may still publish the section using another name.
Rex Heinke, a Los Angeles attorney for Dow Jones, said: "We believe that the decision is wrong and we will be seeking immediate relief in the California Court of Appeal in Sacramento."

He said Dow Jones would seek a stay of Warren's order until an appeal could be heard and would ask the appeals court to rule on the stay before next Wednesday when the next edition of the weekly California section is due. But Dow Jones would certainly obey the preliminary injunction if it was not stayed, he added.

Heinke said "California Journal" has no exclusive right to the name because a third party had already registered it. He said "California Journal" was a generic name and therefore not a protectable trademark and he said the journal's use of the name would not create confusion.

Tom Hoeber, publisher of the "California Journal," which has a circulation of 15,000 compared with The Wall Street Journal's 1.9 million, said on Thursday he was very excited by the judge's ruling. "At the moment we're feeling like David who just felled the giant," he said.

Warren, son of the former U.S. chief justice, said in his written ruling that "California Journal" had a "protectable interest" in the exclusive use of its name. He said the public had come to associate the name with the monthly magazine and The Wall Street Journal's use of it "creates a likelihood of confusion" among the public.
